concept.name: Database Sharding & Range Partitioning
concept.tagline: Horizontally partition massive database tables across multiple database instances using shard keys.

spark.summary: Sharding splits a monolithic database into independent database nodes (shards). Each row is routed to a shard based on a shard key.
spark.keyTakeaway: Select high-cardinality, evenly distributed shard keys (e.g. user_id) to avoid hotspot shards.

concept.whyItMatters: When a single database server hits CPU, RAM, or 10TB disk limits, horizontal sharding spreads data across 100 servers.
whenNotToUse: Small datasets (<100GB) where vertical scaling is cheaper.
keyPoints: Hash-based Sharding hashes shard key modulo N to assign rows evenly.
Range-based Sharding assigns ranges (e.g. A-F, G-M) to shards.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 Hash vs Range Sharding Router Architecture

When a single database instance exhausts vertical disk I/O, storage capacity, and connection memory, **Horizontal Sharding** splits datasets across multiple independent database nodes. The foundational engineering decision is choosing between **Hash-Based Sharding** and **Range-Based Sharding**.

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "Stateless Shard Router & Database Partitions",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "app", "label": "Application Services", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "router", "label": "Shard Router (Vitess / Mongos)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "shard1", "label": "Shard 1 (Hash 00-3F)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "shard2", "label": "Shard 2 (Hash 40-7F)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "shard3", "label": "Shard 3 (Hash 80-FF)", "type": "database" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "app", "to": "router", "label": "1. Query with Shard Key" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard1", "label": "2. Single-Shard Point Route" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard2", "label": "3. Scatter-Gather (Non-Key Query)" }
  ]
}
```

### ⚖️ Hash-Based vs Range-Based Sharding

| Strategy | How Keys Are Mapped | Strengths | Failure Mode / Vulnerability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hash-Based** | `MurmurHash3(shard_key) % NumShards` | Perfectly uniform distribution; eliminates write bottlenecks | Range scans (`WHERE date BETWEEN x AND y`) require expensive **Scatter-Gather** to all shards |
| **Range-Based** | Continuous key intervals (`[A-D]`, `[E-H]`) | Fast, local range scans within single shards | Hot spots on sequential keys (e.g. `timestamp_id` routes 100% of current writes to the newest shard) |

### 🛡️ Mitigating Hot Shards via Key Salting

If a single tenant (e.g. a viral social media account or high-volume merchant) overwhelms a single shard, pure hash sharding still concentrates writes onto one node. Production architectures apply **Key Salting**:

```sql
-- Composite Shard Key with 10 Pseudo-Buckets:
shard_key = user_id || '_' || (murmur_hash(transaction_id) % 10)
```

Writes for the viral user are dispersed uniformly across 10 distinct shards. Read operations query the 10 buckets in parallel and merge results in the stateless router tier.

questions.title: Shard Key Hotspot Prevention
questions.prompt: Why is selecting a low-cardinality column like 'country_code' as a primary database shard key considered a dangerous architectural pitfall?

options.text: Low-cardinality keys require double the RAM per shard node.
options.explanation: Low cardinality affects data distribution across shards, not per-node RAM allocation.

options.text: Low-cardinality keys create severe data skew, concentrating millions of records onto a few hotspot shards while leaving others underutilized.
options.explanation: Correct! Low cardinality forces large volumes of traffic onto single hotspot shard databases.

rubric.excellent: Explains data skew and un-balanced traffic distribution caused by low-cardinality shard keys.
rubric.gap: Confuses cardinality with memory allocation.

questions.sampleSolution: Low-cardinality keys like country_code force all data for large nations onto single hotspot shards. Use high-cardinality keys like user_id.
questions.explanation: High cardinality keys combined with uniform hash functions guarantee even row distribution across N database shards.
